pathophysiology.summary: Bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz. Non-variceal causes (mainly peptic ulcer disease from H. pylori, NSAIDs or aspirin) are most common; variceal bleeding results from portal hypertension in cirrhosis and carries higher mortality.
keyMechanisms: Peptic ulcer: acid–pepsin erosion through a vessel; 'high-risk stigmata' (active bleeding, visible vessel, adherent clot) predict rebleeding.
Varices: portal hypertension diverts blood through fragile oesophageal or gastric collaterals; bleeding is often torrential, and patients are prone to infection, encephalopathy and kidney injury.
Haemoglobin falls late (haemodilution takes hours); urea rises because blood is digested and absorbed.
Antithrombotics (aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitors, warfarin, DOACs) and coagulopathy of liver disease worsen bleeding.

symptoms: Melaena (black tarry stool); fresh rectal blood with shock if bleeding is brisk.
Epigastric pain, NSAID/aspirin/anticoagulant use, alcohol or known liver disease.
physicalSigns: Tachycardia, hypotension, postural drop, cool peripheries (hypovolaemia).
Stigmata of chronic liver disease: jaundice, ascites, spider naevi, splenomegaly (suspect varices).
redFlags: Haemodynamic instability despite resuscitation → major haemorrhage protocol and critical care

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fresh red blood per rectum without shock; brisk upper bleed can mimic it — urea:creatinine ratio and GBS help.
No blood on testing; normal haemodynamics.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: Low haemoglobin (may be normal early); low platelets in liver disease.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Transfuse red cells if Hb below 70 g/L (target 70–100 g/L); higher threshold in ischaemic heart disease or instability. Platelets if actively bleeding and below 50 × 10⁹/L.

references.title: NICE CG141: Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s: management

clinicalManagement.title: Resuscitate
actions: IV access, IV fluids for all; unstable: 500 mL crystalloid bolus in under 15 min (BSG).
Restrictive transfusion: trigger Hb below 70 g/L, target 70–100 g/L (higher trigger in ischaemic heart disease or instability).
Ongoing instability: activate major haemorrhage protocol (blood, platelets, clotting factors) and critical care review.
Platelets if actively bleeding and below 50 × 10⁹/L; do not give platelets if stable and not bleeding.

clinicalManagement.title: Risk-stratify
actions: Calculate GBS. GBS 0–1: consider outpatient management with early endoscopy follow-up.

clinicalManagement.title: Antithrombotics and reversal
actions: Continue low-dose aspirin for secondary prevention (stop other NSAIDs).
Interrupt P2Y12 inhibitors until haemostasis — if coronary stents, decide with cardiology.
Interrupt warfarin; if actively bleeding give PCC (MOH: dose by INR — e.g. INR 2–2.5: 0.9–1.3 mL/kg Octaplex; maximum single dose 3000 IU) plus vitamin K 5–10 mg IV.

Interrupt DOAC; life-threatening bleeding: idarucizumab (dabigatran) or andexanet alfa (apixaban/rivaroxaban) where available; seek haematology advice. MOH protocol lists PCC for life-threatening DOAC bleeding.

clinicalManagement.title: Suspected variceal bleeding (cirrhosis)
actions: Terlipressin 2 mg IV four times a day (BSG); stop after definitive haemostasis or 5 days (NICE). Caution in ischaemic heart or peripheral vascular disease.
IV antibiotics: ceftriaxone 1 g IV every 24 h (MOH prophylaxis in cirrhosis with GI bleeding); oral step-down amoxicillin–clavulanate 500 mg q12h when stable.
Endoscopy: band ligation for oesophageal varices; cyanoacrylate for gastric varices; TIPS if not controlled.

clinicalManagement.title: Endoscopy and non-variceal treatment
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 24 h (immediately after resuscitation if unstable)
actions: No PPI before endoscopy for suspected non-variceal bleeding (NICE).
Endoscopic therapy: mechanical (clips) ± adrenaline, thermal + adrenaline, or fibrin/thrombin + adrenaline — never adrenaline alone.
High-risk stigmata after endoscopy: high-dose IV PPI (e.g. 80 mg bolus then 8 mg/h for 72 h, or intermittent IV / high-dose oral PPI as alternatives).
Rebleeding: repeat endoscopy; unstable rebleed → interventional radiology, or surgery if IR is not promptly available.

regimens.duration: Until haemostasis or up to 5 days
adjustments: Caution: ischaemic heart disease, peripheral vascular disease

regimens.duration: Switch to oral when stable and bleeding controlled after 48 h
adjustments: Severe beta-lactam allergy: ciprofloxacin per MOH

adjustments: Intermittent IV or high-dose oral PPI are acceptable alternatives (BSG)

regimens.dose: By INR: 2–2.5 → 0.9–1.3 mL/kg; 2.5–3 → 1.3–1.6 mL/kg; 3–3.5 → 1.6–1.9 mL/kg; above 3.5 → above 1.9 mL/kg (max single dose 3000 IU)
adjustments: Give vitamin K 5–10 mg IV with PCC
Contraindicated in chronic liver disease coagulopathy and oesophageal varices (MOH)

medicationPlan.note: PCC is contraindicated for coagulopathy of chronic liver disease and in oesophageal varices per the MOH reversal protocol — use FFP/cryoprecipitate per NICE in these patients. Check SFDA registration and formulary (terlipressin, andexanet, idarucizumab availability varies).

learningObjectives: Recognise, investigate and manage acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in the emergency department.
pitfalls: Using PCC for liver-disease coagulopathy or varices (contraindicated per MOH).
Stopping aspirin without a reason; no restart plan for antithrombotics.
keyPoints: GBS 0–1 can be managed as outpatients.
Suspected varices: terlipressin + antibiotics before endoscopy.
Endoscopy within 24 h; immediately if unstable.
No PPI before endoscopy (NICE); high-dose PPI after high-risk stigmata.
